- Overestimate prices when sentiment is high (especially >0.5) — reduce forecast slightly to align with mean reversion.
- Underestimate prices when sentiment is low (especially <0.3) — increase forecast modestly to account for potential rebound.
- Overshoot after sharp price spikes — cap forecast at 1–2% below peak if sentiment remains neutral or cooling.
- Lagged price movements often over-predict short-term reversals — adjust forecast downward by 0.5–1.5% for 3–5 day horizons.
- When sentiment is rising sharply, model tends to overreact — dampen forecast slope to avoid premature peak.
- For 30-day forecasts, if recent 5-day average is rising, reduce forecast by 0.5–1.5% to avoid overconfidence in momentum.
- If sentiment is consistently above 0.7 over 3+ days, reduce forecast by 1–2% to avoid overestimating bullish momentum.
- If sentiment drops sharply after a spike, reduce forecast by 1–2% to avoid “sell the rumor” bias.
- Mean reversion bias: if forecast is >10% above recent 10-day average, reduce by 1–2% per day until convergence.
- Avoid forecasting “new highs” when sentiment is low — cap forecast at 1–2% below recent 5-day high if sentiment <0.4.
